title: Ace Combat 8 Mission 28 S Rank Walkthrough
description: Ace Combat 8 Mission 28 S Rank guide: objectives, loadout planning, attack priorities, replay checklist, and common mistakes to avoid.

hero.heading: Ace Combat 8 Mission 28 S Rank Guide
hero.lead: Protect Cima Island by intercepting bombers, use the island airstrip to replenish ammunition, then prepare for the final Shadow Squadron engagement. Build your S Rank attempt around a repeatable clear and compare the results screen after each replay.
quickRoute: Intercept bombers threatening the base before chasing escorts.
Rearm during a safe opening and keep checking approaching formations.
Finish the aerial battle, then resolve the final dogfight with deliberate shots.

sections.heading: Mission 28 Quick Strategy
paragraphs: A Thousand Points of Light is an air-defense mission. The useful planning distinction is between enemies that threaten the defended base and enemies that distract you from that job. A fighter behind you can demand an evasive maneuver without becoming the next target you must chase across the map. Keep returning your attention to the objective after defending yourself.

For a first clear, learn how the battle develops before adding rank ambitions. For a replay, decide which part of your previous attempt needs improvement. A missed bomber, an unnecessary journey to rearm, and a drawn-out dogfight need different fixes. Buying another aircraft before identifying that problem can leave the same inefficient route intact.

sections.heading: Recommended Plane and Special Weapons
paragraphs: Choose an air-to-air loadout you can fly accurately through both interception and close combat. An aircraft that makes the early formations easy can still be awkward in the final encounter. Start with a familiar fighter or multirole jet and inspect its special-weapon choices in the hangar. Surface attack equipment contributes little to an operation dominated by aircraft.

Think of your weapon budget as a plan for separate jobs. Multi-target air weapons are an option for formations; a focused air weapon or gun pass serves a different purpose against an evasive opponent. Confirm that your own aircraft supports the desired option before purchasing anything. Good guidance cannot rescue a shot fired from a poor angle, and ammunition capacity cannot compensate for repeated misses.

subsections.heading: Opening: defend the base
paragraphs: Make the incoming bomber force your first concern. Choose an intercept that lets you arrive ahead of the threat instead of following it toward the base. After attacking, check whether the selected aircraft was destroyed before moving on. A damaged bomber remains an objective risk. Do not mistake a missile impact for a completed interception.

subsections.heading: Continuing battle: manage weapons and rearm
paragraphs: Reinforcements make situational awareness more valuable than a rigid memorized compass direction. Read the radar after each engagement and identify which bomber group needs attention next. The Cima Island airstrip provides a rearming opportunity. Use it while the defense is stable; avoid waiting until an urgent interception begins with an empty weapon inventory.

subsections.heading: Final encounter: settle the dogfight
paragraphs: The late Shadow Squadron encounter changes the task from formation management to fighting evasive aircraft. Stop treating every lock as a firing opportunity. Reposition, build a controlled approach and use the gun when tracking is steady. If a target breaks sharply, recover your position before committing another shot. The final engagement deserves ammunition and concentration saved from the earlier battle.

sections.heading: How to Improve Your S Rank Attempt
paragraphs: Use the debrief to compare completed runs on the same difficulty and game version. Record the displayed score, completion time and rank; do not substitute the opening objective quota for an S Rank cutoff. Those are different questions. A successful mission proves that the objective was completed, while an S result is a separate replay goal.

Choose one change for the next attempt. If the defense broke down, improve interception first. If the route was safe but slow, identify unnecessary travel or the encounter that consumed the most time. If many missiles missed, try better launch angles before increasing difficulty. Keeping the other settings consistent makes the comparison useful rather than leaving you to guess why the result changed.

subsections.heading: Repeatable Replay Checklist
paragraphs: Before launch, write down the aircraft, weapon setup and one improvement you want to test. During the run, protect the base, verify kills and rearm with a purpose. After completion, save the result and note the phase that cost the most time. Repeat the same setup until the change produces a stable improvement. A checklist is useful only if it remains short enough to follow under pressure.

sections.heading: Common Mission 28 Failure Points
paragraphs: When the base takes damage while you are busy with fighters, the problem is target selection. Break away and recheck the bomber approach. When you run out of ammunition, the problem may be missed shots or a late rearm decision. When the final fight drags on, repeated firing from a bad position can make the problem worse rather than solve it.

Give yourself room to recover from every attack. A close pass is worthwhile only when you can leave it without a collision or a prolonged defensive scramble. Keep a practical distinction between evading a threat and following that threat. Your route should return to the defended objective after the immediate danger passes.

sections.heading: Mission 28 and MRP Farming
paragraphs: A long aerial battle can produce a substantial results screen without being your most efficient currency route. Include selection, loading, rearming, final combat and any failures when comparing a replay. A shorter mission you finish consistently may serve a purchase goal better. Keep rank practice and earning efficiency as separate measurements, even when one sortie advances both.

Once the route is comfortable, compare several full attempts rather than the best single payout. If you are still learning the final encounter, treat that time as practice. It is useful progress, but it should not disappear from a farming calculation.

faq.answer: Intercept bombers threatening Cima Island. Deal with escorts when they obstruct the defense or the objective changes.

faq.question: What score guarantees S Rank?
faq.answer: Compare the rank, time and score displayed after your completed replay. This guide does not prescribe a fixed cutoff or equate the mission objective quota with S Rank.

faq.question: Can I replenish ammunition?
faq.answer: The mission provides rearming at the Cima Island airstrip. Plan the return around the current bomber threat.

faq.question: Which aircraft should I use?
faq.answer: Choose a controllable air-to-air aircraft whose available weapons cover formations and evasive fighters. Check its actual hangar options.

faq.question: Should I farm MRP while learning the final fight?
faq.answer: Learning is useful, but count every attempt and its full duration when measuring earnings. Compare it with a reliable shorter replay.

title: Ace Combat 8 Mission 16 Walkthrough & Tips
description: Ace Combat 8 Mission 16 walkthrough with objective order, ship identification, UAV phase tips, recommended loadouts, and mission fixes.

hero.heading: Ace Combat 8 Mission 16 Walkthrough
hero.lead: Mission 16, Singer, asks you to identify hostile container ships among civilian traffic. Look for the combination of three cranes and a sun emblem, attack confirmed targets, and switch to the climbing Explosive UAVs if they launch.
quickRoute: Inspect the shipping area before firing at an unconfirmed vessel.
Identify the crane arrangement and sun marking together.
If Explosive UAVs launch, intercept the highest threats first.

sections.heading: Mission 16 Objectives at a Glance
paragraphs: This sortie is an identification problem before it becomes a weapons problem. Ships in view are not automatically authorized targets. Slow the decision down enough to inspect the relevant vessel and then make a deliberate attack. A quick missile launch at the wrong ship is less useful than a slightly longer approach that gives you a clear visual check.

The later UAV threat changes that rhythm. Once drones are climbing, continuing the ship search can consume the time you need for interception. Read the new objective as soon as it appears. Your earlier surface-target plan must yield to the active aerial threat rather than continuing simply because it was the plan at launch.

sections.heading: Best Aircraft and Weapons for Mission 16
paragraphs: Prepare for both surface targets and a possible air interception phase. A familiar multirole aircraft is a reasonable starting point because the decision requires more than raw anti-ship firepower. You need enough control to inspect a vessel and enough aerial capability to respond promptly after an objective change. Select weapons after checking the exact options in your current hangar.

A multi-target air weapon can help when several drones are available to engage from one approach. It does not remove the need to acquire sensible locks. Avoid committing your entire weapon selection to ships and then discovering that the airborne threat requires repeated standard-missile passes. Conversely, a costly aircraft upgrade is unnecessary if your current setup can perform both jobs reliably.

subsections.heading: Locate and inspect the container ships
paragraphs: Enter the shipping area and make a pass that gives you a clear view of each candidate. Inspect one vessel at a time. Keep the crane arrangement and emblem in mind together; recognizing only one feature is a reason to look again. Avoid trying to count details while also forcing a very steep attack angle. A clean inspection pass makes the following engagement easier.

subsections.heading: Commit to the confirmed targets
paragraphs: Once the visual identification is clear, line up the attack and keep track of which ship you have engaged. Make the distinction between a vessel you inspected, a vessel you damaged and a vessel you destroyed. That prevents repeated passes over a completed target while another candidate remains unresolved. After the attack, check the current objective instead of assuming that a weapon impact ended the stage.

subsections.heading: React to the UAV objective
paragraphs: If the Explosive UAV phase begins, climb and prioritize drones that are already highest. Their movement toward the Space Elevator is the urgent problem. Use the radar to choose your next interception and keep scanning after each kill. Do not keep circling the shipping lane out of habit when the objective has moved into the air.

sections.heading: How to Find the Correct Targets
paragraphs: The visual cue is the combination of three cranes and a sun emblem. Plan an approach that allows both to be inspected. If the emblem is hidden by your angle, turn for another view rather than interpreting an unclear shape as confirmation. This is particularly helpful when several similar vessels occupy the same scene and you are tempted to use position alone.

A useful mental record has three states: unchecked, confirmed and cleared. Move a ship between those states only after the relevant action. You do not need an invented coordinate list to apply this method. You need to avoid letting a familiar-looking silhouette become a substitute for the identification task the mission presents.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes and Fixes
paragraphs: If every container ship looks the same, separate inspection from attack. Give yourself a stable view before selecting a weapon. If you lose track of your target, return to the identification cue instead of firing at the nearest vessel. If the UAVs get ahead of you, the next replay should improve the transition between jobs before making the ship phase faster.

A loadout mismatch can resemble an aiming problem. When you consistently need too many aerial passes, inspect your air weapon options and test one adjustment. When you struggle to see a ship marking, aircraft handling and approach angle deserve attention before firepower. Buy a specific solution to a repeated difficulty rather than spending MRP on a general impression that your plane is weak.

sections.heading: Replay and Rank Tips
paragraphs: During your first successful run, learn the visual check and the objective transition. During a rank replay, reduce repeated inspection passes without skipping confirmation. Save the results screen and note whether your delay came from searching, attacking or climbing to intercept. That gives the next attempt a concrete purpose.

Keep the same difficulty while comparing changes. There is no reason to interpret a different result as proof that a new aircraft helped when several other settings also changed. For currency planning, include the complete repeat loop and failed attempts. A short successful sortie can be useful, but the rate comes from your recorded rewards and elapsed time.

faq.answer: Look for three cranes together with a sun emblem. Use a clear visual approach and confirm both details before attacking.

faq.answer: Switch to aerial interception and prioritize the drones already highest as they climb toward the Space Elevator.

faq.answer: Choose a loadout that can deal with confirmed surface targets and respond to the UAV phase. A practical multirole setup can cover both jobs.

faq.answer: Reduce unnecessary inspection passes, track cleared ships and improve the transition to the aerial objective. Compare completed runs on the same difficulty.

title: Ace Combat 8 Mission 26 Walkthrough & Loadout
description: Ace Combat 8 Mission 26 guide with objective priorities, fleet-defense tactics, aircraft loadouts, combat phases, and troubleshooting tips.

hero.heading: Ace Combat 8 Mission 26 Walkthrough
hero.lead: Mission 26, Crossing Fleets, combines the opening fleet battle with a later high-altitude encounter. Clear priority threats while protecting allied vessels, keep an air-capable loadout ready, and follow the changed objective through the scripted encounter and return sequence.
quickRoute: Build the required objective score while responding to fleet danger.
Recheck the radar and current orders after every attack pass.
Switch to the high-altitude encounter when ordered, then follow the return objective.

sections.heading: Mission 26 Quick Answer and Objectives
paragraphs: Approach the opening as a battle you must manage, rather than a list of targets you can finish in any order. The mission combines scoring with keeping the allied force safe. An attractive surface target can wait when an incoming threat demands intervention. Your next attack should come from the present objective state, not simply from whichever enemy is already selected.

The later aerial encounter is a separate planning concern. Save enough attention and aircraft capability for the change. Clearing the opening does not mean you can ignore the next instruction or continue farming unrelated targets. Listen for the objective transition, locate the new threat and adjust your approach before firing.

sections.heading: Best Plane and Special Weapon Loadout
paragraphs: A mixed mission benefits from a mixed plan. Before launch, inspect which surface weapon your aircraft can equip and what aerial option remains available. A specialist attacker may help in the opening, but you still need to handle the later airborne target. A familiar multirole aircraft is worth considering when a more specialized purchase would leave that second job awkward.

Think about attack approaches as well as weapon labels. A surface weapon that works well on a clean approach may be difficult to use if you repeatedly enter from an obstructed angle. An air weapon also needs spacing and a usable firing opportunity. Select a setup that lets you keep responding to fleet reports instead of requiring a long reset after every engagement.

subsections.heading: Opening: make progress without neglecting the fleet
paragraphs: Attack targets that advance the opening objective and watch the status of allied vessels. After each pass, read the radar and mission messages again. That brief check helps you avoid a common defense-mission habit: repeatedly attacking the same convenient area while a different threat moves toward the objective. Confirm destruction before counting a target as cleared.

subsections.heading: Fleet defense: redirect when the situation changes
paragraphs: Treat a fleet warning as a reason to reconsider your next target. If an aircraft or other marked threat is endangering an ally, intercept it before resuming less urgent surface attacks. Do not assume the fleet is secure simply because your score is progressing well. Maintain a usable escape path from each pass so you can change direction without a prolonged defensive scramble.

subsections.heading: High-altitude encounter and return
paragraphs: A high-altitude attacker appears after the opening battle. Follow the instruction to engage and react to its attack warnings instead of expecting a conventional surface-target cleanup. The encounter includes a scripted story transition. Continue following the current orders afterward, including the return sequence; do not treat an apparent interruption as proof that the mission is broken.

sections.heading: Threat Priorities and Fleet Protection
paragraphs: Use consequence and urgency to choose targets. A threat about to reach an ally matters more than a distant target that offers a convenient shot. After resolving the urgent problem, return to the opening objective and choose a route that avoids unnecessary travel. This is a decision rule, not a claim that every replay presents exactly the same target order.

It helps to define what a successful pass should accomplish before you begin it. Are you removing a threat, adding needed score or repositioning for the next instruction? If a pass does none of those, it may be consuming time without helping the mission. Keep weapons for the problems your setup is designed to solve rather than firing every special weapon whenever a lock appears.

sections.heading: Common Mission 26 Failures
paragraphs: If allied vessels are lost while your score rises, revise your target priorities. Check objective reports more often and shorten the detours that leave the fleet unattended. If the opening score stalls, verify that your attacks are actually destroying targets and that the chosen weapon suits the surface job. If you reach the later encounter poorly equipped, revise the whole-sortie loadout rather than optimizing the opening in isolation.

When a dramatic late event occurs, read the new instruction before restarting. A scripted transition can look like a failed attack if you expect every enemy to behave like an ordinary target. Keep flying safely and give the mission sequence a chance to advance. Restart to correct a real failure, rather than merely because the story did something unexpected.

sections.heading: Replay, Rank and Completion Tips
paragraphs: Separate learning the objective sequence from improving the result. On a learning attempt, note when your attention must shift away from surface clearance. On a replay, refine the attack route while keeping those transitions intact. Record the completed result rather than judging the run solely by the opening score.

A useful comparison changes one variable: the chosen surface weapon, a particular approach or the time spent responding to a fleet warning. Keep difficulty and other loadout choices stable while testing it. If you are also preparing for the later Mission 28 air battle, use these replays to practice returning to the objective after evasive maneuvers. That skill transfers even though the target mix changes.

title: Ace Combat 8 MRP Farming: Fast Routes & Tips
description: Find practical Ace Combat 8 MRP farming routes, compare rewards per minute, avoid wasted aircraft-tree purchases, and plan better replays.

hero.heading: Ace Combat 8 MRP Farming Guide
hero.lead: Farm MRP by repeating a mission you can finish reliably, recording the currency actually banked and timing the entire repeat loop. Compare total MRP per minute across several attempts, including failures, before committing to a route.
quickRoute: Choose one aircraft-tree purchase and budget its prerequisites.
Test an available replay with the same loadout and difficulty.
Divide total banked MRP by total elapsed minutes, then compare another route.

sections.heading: How MRP Works in Ace Combat 8
paragraphs: MRP is the campaign currency used to unlock additional aircraft. Treat the results screen as your record of what a sortie earned, and the Aircraft Tree as your record of what a purchase requires. Mission score, mission rank and spendable currency answer different questions. A high score is not a currency amount you should enter into a farming comparison.

Campaign and ACE COMBAT ONLINE have separate progression and save data. Begin by checking which mode contains the item you want. A campaign currency plan should serve a campaign purchase; it is not a shortcut around an Online resource requirement. This simple check prevents a long grinding session aimed at the wrong progression system.

steps.heading: Choose a destination
steps.description: Identify the aircraft, weapon or part that solves your current problem. Keep that destination visible while deciding whether optional purchases are worth delaying it.

steps.heading: Budget the route
steps.description: Trace the required nodes from your owned equipment to the destination. Add the displayed prices of unowned prerequisites rather than using only the final aircraft price.

steps.heading: Select a reliable replay
steps.description: Start with an available mission you know how to finish. Use a loadout that fits its actual targets and keep the difficulty steady during the first comparison.

steps.heading: Measure the complete loop
steps.description: Start timing before selection and stop when you are ready to select the next run. Record banked currency after completion and keep failed attempts in the elapsed time.

steps.heading: Compare and reassess
steps.description: Repeat several attempts, then test a different route. Recalculate after a meaningful aircraft or weapon change and stop farming when the planned purchase is affordable.

sections.heading: Best Missions to Test for MRP
paragraphs: Missions 7, 24 and 28 are useful candidates discussed in current farming guides, rather than guaranteed winners. The right comparison depends on what you have unlocked and how consistently you finish each route. Treat another player’s large payout as an invitation to test, not a promise of the same rate in your hangar.

Include a shorter mission you already know well. That establishes a baseline against which a more complex replay must earn its place. A mission with many targets can lose its advantage through extra travel, rearming or a difficult final encounter. Avoid changing both difficulty and route at once if you want to know which change helped.

sections.heading: MRP Per Minute Comparison
paragraphs: Use total banked MRP divided by total elapsed minutes. Count the entire session, including briefing, loading, rearming, results screens, retries and unsuccessful attempts. If a failure banks no currency, record no earned currency for that attempt but retain its time. Otherwise, an unreliable route can appear faster simply because you discarded its worst results.

Illustration only: suppose a test session banks 120,000 MRP in 12 minutes. Its rate is 10,000 MRP per minute. A second hypothetical session banks 150,000 in 20 minutes, or 7,500 per minute. These numbers are arithmetic examples, not game payouts. The first session is more efficient despite the second showing a larger total reward.

Keep a small log with route, difficulty, aircraft, weapon setup, elapsed time and earned currency. Use several runs to reduce the effect of one unusually good or bad attempt. If results vary widely, reliability is still part of the decision. Choose a slightly lower but stable rate when the supposedly faster option often fails.

sections.heading: MRP Spending Priorities
paragraphs: Spend to remove a specific constraint. If a needed weapon is already supported by an owned aircraft, compare that purchase with the full route to a new plane. If your problem is controlling the approach, another weapon may do little to help. A useful purchase changes a repeated mission difficulty rather than merely making the aircraft list longer.

For a destination aircraft, distinguish mandatory connecting nodes from optional equipment. Check each displayed price and mark what you already own. Keep a reserve for the loadout you intend to use instead of exhausting the balance on an airframe that still needs another purchase. Reopen the budget after any prerequisite is acquired so you know the remaining gap.

sections.heading: Early vs Mid vs Late Campaign Farming
paragraphs: Early in the campaign, story progression can be more valuable than repeating a mission indefinitely. It expands the set of operations you can compare and helps you understand which roles your aircraft must cover. Pause to farm when a specific purchase will resolve a real obstacle, then return to progress once that goal is met.

In the middle of a campaign, reassess your owned equipment before opening several new branches. Later, when replay options are available, compare familiar routes systematically and combine earning with completion goals only when those goals do not make the route unreliable. Rank practice is worthwhile, but keep its learning time in your currency calculation rather than hiding it.

faq.question: What is the fastest MRP farming mission?
faq.answer: Test several available missions using total banked MRP divided by complete loop time. The best route depends on your equipment and reliable completion rate.

faq.question: Should I count loading and retries?
faq.answer: Yes. Count all elapsed time required to repeat the route, including failed attempts.

faq.question: Is a high mission score the same as MRP?
faq.answer: No. Record the earned campaign currency from the results screen instead of treating score or rank as a payout.

faq.question: How much should I save for an aircraft?
faq.answer: Add every unowned required node along the route plus the equipment you intend to use. Read the current prices in the Aircraft Tree.

faq.question: Can Campaign MRP replace Online progression?
faq.answer: Campaign and ACE COMBAT ONLINE use separate progression and save data. Check the requirements in the mode containing your intended purchase.

faq.question: When should I stop farming?
faq.answer: Stop when the planned purchase is affordable or when another available route proves more efficient. Avoid an open-ended grind without a purchase goal.

subsections.heading: Mission 16: an identification problem
paragraphs: If you can fly and shoot but still cannot progress, begin with the visual inspection task. The Mission 16 guide separates recognizing the hostile vessel from attacking it, then explains the shift to the airborne objective. Use it to correct a decision problem before assuming that more damage or a more expensive aircraft is the answer.

subsections.heading: Mission 26: a priority problem
paragraphs: A battle with several useful targets can tempt you to chase score while overlooking the objective that needs protection. The Mission 26 guide organizes the sortie around what deserves attention now and how the task changes later. Use it when your opening route works in isolation but the whole operation still breaks down.

subsections.heading: Mission 28: a replay consistency problem
paragraphs: A long defense can be cleared without producing the rank you want. The Mission 28 guide helps you separate objective safety, ammunition planning and the final encounter. Use completed results to decide which part to improve rather than treating every lower rank as evidence that the entire loadout is wrong.

sections.heading: How to Prepare for a New Mission
paragraphs: Read the briefing with three questions in mind: what must be completed, what must survive and what could force a change in target priority? Then inspect your aircraft choices. Keep the most important objective in view when choosing weapons instead of selecting a favorite weapon first and hoping the mission will suit it.

Make a short preparation note. Name the dominant target type, identify any restriction displayed by the game and decide how you will handle a secondary threat. You do not need a complicated spreadsheet for a first clear. You need a reason for each major equipment choice and a plan that remains understandable when the objective changes.

Before buying, test whether an owned aircraft can cover the task with another supported weapon. An unnecessary branch can delay the plane you actually want later. If a purchase is needed, connect it to the specific failure you are solving: surface clearance, aerial interception, ammunition pressure or difficult handling.

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Aircraft for Mission Types
paragraphs: Use the mission’s job as the starting point for aircraft selection. Air-heavy operations reward an aerial setup; surface-heavy operations need weapons suited to the targets; mixed sorties require a fallback when the dominant target type changes. The class name is useful, but the actual weapons you can equip determine whether the setup works.

Comfort matters during a first clear. A plane that responds predictably can reduce missed approaches and recovery time even if a different aircraft appears more impressive in a recommendation list. Compare the entire sortie with both setups before concluding that a purchase improved it. Include any restriction shown in the mission menu rather than assuming all aircraft are selectable everywhere.

sections.heading: Replay Missions for S Rank and MRP
paragraphs: Define the goal of a replay before you launch. A rank attempt asks how efficiently you can complete the operation under the chosen settings. A farming attempt asks how much currency you bank over the entire repeat loop. These goals can overlap, but one useful result does not prove the other.

For rank improvement, record the displayed time, score and grade after completion. For farming, add the earned MRP and complete elapsed time. Keep failed attempts visible in the farming log. If the next replay is a practice run for one awkward phase, label it as practice in your own notes so you do not compare it with an optimized currency route.

Change one part of the plan between attempts. A new aircraft, new weapons and higher difficulty together can make a result difficult to interpret. A controlled comparison helps you preserve what already works while improving the real weak point.

faq.answer: They can overlap, but rank planning and currency efficiency use different measurements. Record the result relevant to your goal.

faq.question: How do I diagnose a failed sortie?
faq.answer: Identify whether the problem was target selection, objective protection, equipment or execution. Adjust the relevant part of the plan before replacing everything.

hero.lead: Shortlist the F-35C for a flexible multirole role, F-22A for an air-focused role, and Rafale M for a naval multirole option. For an early budget decision, first test the F/A-18C you already own. Choose the aircraft and supported weapons that solve your next mission.

Compare the actual special weapons on the aircraft you can acquire.
Budget the full prerequisite route before buying a new plane.

sections.heading: Best Planes at a Glance
paragraphs: A useful aircraft shortlist begins with jobs rather than a universal tier ranking. The publisher’s aircraft roster establishes the roles below. The recommendations are starting points for choosing and testing a loadout, not measured claims that one airframe wins every encounter. Purchase prices are omitted here because the connecting route and your owned equipment also affect the budget.

Check the variant carefully. Aircraft with related names may offer different options, and a recommendation for one model is not a reason to assume another carries the same weapon. Open the hangar entry, inspect available equipment and check the mission’s selection screen before committing MRP.

sections.heading: Best All-Round Aircraft
paragraphs: The F-35C is a sensible aircraft to compare when your missions change between air and surface targets. Its multirole classification makes it an appropriate shortlist entry, but that role alone does not select the weapon for you. Check the specific loadout you intend to use and compare it with an owned multirole aircraft on a familiar mission.

Ask whether the upgrade solves a repeated problem. If your current aircraft clears surface targets well but struggles with the aerial transition, a different weapon or a better approach may already address it. If both jobs are consistently awkward, a broader aircraft comparison becomes more useful. Keep one reliable setup while testing the new purchase so you can distinguish improvement from unfamiliar handling.

sections.heading: Best Air-to-Air Aircraft
paragraphs: The F-22A belongs on an air-focused shortlist. Choose a fighter when the mission asks you to manage repeated aerial engagements, but evaluate how you use it rather than relying on a class label. Stable tracking, sensible launch angles and recovery space are all part of turning an aerial loadout into a reliable clear.

Before spending, compare the aircraft’s available weapon choices with the enemies causing trouble. Formations and evasive single targets are different jobs. A multi-target option can help you use an aligned approach efficiently, while a close dogfight may demand more controlled firing. Test the setup in a known encounter before treating a recommendation as a guaranteed solution.

sections.heading: Best Planes for Ground and Naval Missions
paragraphs: Rafale M offers a naval multirole option to consider, while an available attacker such as the A-6E provides a surface-role alternative. Inspect the actual surface weapons and launch restrictions before choosing between them. A sortie with an important late air phase may justify a broader setup than a mission devoted mostly to surface clearance.

Do not treat every ship or ground target as the same weapons problem. Position, approach and the need to return quickly to an ally can change which option feels practical. A surface weapon that requires repeated awkward passes may be less helpful than a simpler setup you can use accurately. Compare complete sorties rather than the damage impression from one impressive hit.

sections.heading: Best Early-Campaign Aircraft
paragraphs: For an early budget choice, start with the aircraft already in your hangar. The F/A-18C is a multirole entry worth evaluating before you commit to a new branch. Buying early is useful when a purchase solves a concrete obstacle; buying simply because you want to replace a starter can consume MRP without improving the next mission.

List the job you need to perform, the supported equipment you already have and the smallest upgrade that could help. Test that adjustment first. If the remaining problem is handling, spend practice time on the approach before treating a more expensive airframe as the answer. Affordability should include the whole route from owned nodes, not just a low price beside a tempting model.

sections.heading: Aircraft Tree, MRP and Purchase Planning
paragraphs: Trace the route to one destination aircraft and write down the prices of unowned required nodes. Include the equipment you plan to use once the aircraft is acquired. Keep optional purchases separate so you can see exactly what delays the destination. An aircraft is not ready for your intended job merely because you can afford its final node.

When a mission becomes difficult, revisit the purchase goal. The best next plane might differ from the plane you eventually want for collection or a later replay. It is reasonable to buy a smaller targeted solution now if it gets the campaign moving again. Measure that decision by useful progress rather than the prestige of the aircraft name.

sections.heading: Best Loadouts for Difficult Missions
paragraphs: Mission 16 tests recognition and the transition from surface targets to airborne threats. Build for both jobs and remember that firepower cannot identify the correct ship. Mission 26 calls for opening clearance and attention to a later aerial encounter. Choose a setup for the whole operation rather than treating the first battle as the entire sortie.

Mission 28 emphasizes air defense and a late dogfight. Compare air weapon options and plan ammunition use around the rearming opportunity. In each case, the detailed walkthrough should guide the buying decision: first understand why the attempt failed, then choose equipment that addresses that failure. Do not purchase three different aircraft before testing one focused change.

sections.heading: Common Aircraft Buying Mistakes
paragraphs: Avoid opening several unrelated branches at once, assuming a recommendation includes every prerequisite or confusing an airframe’s role with its currently equipped weapon. Also avoid judging a new purchase after an unfamiliar mission that changed several other variables. Use a known replay for a fair comparison.

A practical buying decision can be written in one sentence: this purchase helps this mission because it supplies this capability. If you cannot finish that sentence, inspect your owned alternatives again. The aim is a hangar that covers the operations you play, with equipment you can use confidently.

title: Ace Combat 8 Mission 15 Walkthrough & Tips
description: Ace Combat 8 Mission 15 walkthrough with objective priorities, aircraft loadout tips, stage-by-stage strategy, common mistakes, and replay advice.

hero.heading: Ace Combat 8 Mission 15 Walkthrough
hero.lead: Mission 15, Wings of Wax, is an interception battle against Ladon bombers threatening the friendly fleet. Plan where to meet each bomber rather than spending the whole sortie trying to catch it from behind.
quickRoute: Keep the fleet-defense objective active in your planning; do not follow a distant distraction away from the bombers.
Use the Ladons’ turns to shorten your interception path, then select an engine for a controlled attack.
Close the distance before expecting a missile lock through the jamming; save ammunition when no firing solution exists.
After a pass, recover speed and locate the other bomber before committing to another chase.

sections.heading: Mission 15 Quick Route
paragraphs: Begin by locating the fleet and the bombers’ direction of travel. Your first useful action is positioning: turn toward an interception point while retaining enough room to correct your approach. A bomber directly ahead can tempt you into holding the throttle and following its exact path. If the range keeps opening, that approach is consuming time without producing a shot. Break the chase and plan a shorter crossing instead.

Treat each pass as a small sequence: find the bomber, identify the selected component, establish a stable firing line, shoot, and check the result. Do not continue pressing fire simply because the aircraft remains somewhere near the reticle. Decide where your next useful attack will begin before making another large turn. That habit helps protect both ammunition and the fleet.

sections.heading: Objectives and Mission Phases
paragraphs: Wings of Wax is Operation Deal Cards. The central problem is air interception, rather than clearing ground positions. Two Ladons and their jamming change how you approach the fight. Keep the objective display and fleet warnings in view; use them to decide whether there is time to reposition or whether a bomber already threatening the ships needs immediate attention.

The table describes decision points, not additional scripted stages. Let the current target markers tell you when engagement is available. During an opening sequence without a valid target, maneuver into a useful position and preserve ammunition. After a bomber is destroyed, recheck the remaining threat instead of assuming that the same approach will still be safe.

table.caption: Interception decisions
rows: Emptying missiles into an unavailable target
Check the engine target and fire deliberately
Cycling targets while releasing a volley
Read the updated threat and plan a fresh pass
Assuming the battle is already won

sections.heading: Recommended Aircraft and Weapons
paragraphs: Choose an air-focused aircraft you can keep under control at speed. Acceleration helps you recover after turning; useful handling helps you create the next firing opportunity. Compare aircraft that you already own before making an expensive purchase. A faster airframe does not solve an interception route that continually puts you behind the target. Test the route and the aircraft as separate variables.

Use air-to-air special weapons suited to the close engagements you can actually establish. Read the hangar descriptions for your available options, then choose a combination you understand. An impressive nominal range is less helpful when jamming prevents the lock you need. Favor weapons that let you turn a brief, stable window into dependable damage. Keep standard missiles available between special-weapon opportunities rather than spending everything at the first contact.

If ammunition runs low, review missed launches before buying more capacity. Check whether you fired without a completed lock, switched to the wrong component, or launched just as the bomber left your useful angle. Capacity can create room for mistakes, but fixing those mistakes makes every aircraft more effective. The aircraft guide linked below helps compare roles without requiring one specific purchase.

steps.heading: Set up the crossing
steps.description: Watch the bomber’s direction and turn toward the inside of its path. Leave yourself a clear recovery line. If you arrive with too much closure, ease off enough to keep the target in view instead of overshooting and starting another long chase.

steps.heading: Confirm the component
steps.description: When the HUD offers a valid engagement, check the selected component before firing. An engine attack requires the engine to be selected. Keep the aircraft steady long enough to judge the effect; a hurried volley at an unintended weapon mount spends ammunition without advancing the same plan.

steps.heading: Recover and reassess
steps.description: After shooting, clear the immediate danger and recover your position. Locate both the fleet and the remaining bomber threat. If the previous attack became a pursuit with no shots, change the interception angle on the next pass rather than repeating the same turn farther behind.

sections.heading: Threat Priorities and Common Mistakes
paragraphs: A lock that disappears does not mean the mission has stopped progressing. In this fight, jamming is a reason to work on positioning. Use the visible aircraft and its travel direction to establish another close approach, while keeping the terrain and your own attitude readable. Flying deeper into poor visibility with no planned exit makes reacquisition harder and increases the risk of a collision.

If you are repeatedly shot down, identify where it happens. An extended, predictable approach is a different problem from a collision during an aggressive recovery. For the former, shorten your exposure and leave the attack line before you lose control of the engagement. For the latter, allow more space and reduce the amount of correction demanded at the end of the pass. Keep the next attempt focused on that one failure.

Fleet losses should prompt an earlier interception, not an unrelated score chase. Note where you were when the warning arrived. If you were following a bomber away from its next approach, plan your next run from the fleet’s position outward. This keeps your decisions tied to the protected objective.

sections.heading: Replay and Rank Improvement Tips
paragraphs: For a first clear, prioritize a route you can repeat and enough reserve to finish the remaining bomber. For a rank replay, compare where the previous run lost useful firing time. Record the first engagement, missed approaches, and ammunition remaining. Improve one crossing before changing the entire loadout. A route with fewer empty pursuits gives you a clearer basis for assessing the result screen.

Keep optional collection separate from learning the main interception. A detour that adds a target can also change the fleet situation and your next meeting point. After a successful clear, use the mission results to decide whether the next attempt should emphasize cleaner attacks or quicker positioning. Do not treat a suggested route as a guaranteed S Rank threshold.

faq.question: Why can’t I lock onto a Ladon?
faq.answer: The Ladons use jamming. Work toward a closer, stable interception and check the HUD for a valid lock before launching. A longer-range weapon alone does not remove the positioning problem.

faq.question: What should I do when the bomber pulls away?
faq.answer: Stop following its full outside path. Use its direction and next turn to set up a shorter crossing, with enough room to recover if the first shot is missed.

faq.question: Which weapon should I bring to Mission 15?
faq.answer: Choose air-to-air weapons you can use reliably during close approaches. Check your unlocked loadouts and pair a manageable aircraft with enough missile reserve for both bombers.

faq.question: How can I save ammunition?
faq.answer: Confirm the selected component and lock before each volley. Stop firing during an empty pursuit, and judge whether the previous hit worked before spending another special weapon.

faq.question: Should I chase optional targets on my first clear?
faq.answer: Learn the bomber interception and fleet-defense route first. Optional pursuits are easier to evaluate on a separate attempt once you know how much time and ammunition the clear needs.

title: Ace Combat 8 Mission 25 Walkthrough & Strategy
description: Ace Combat 8 Mission 25 guide with a clear objective route, priority targets, recommended loadout choices, common failure points, and replay tips.

hero.heading: Ace Combat 8 Mission 25 Walkthrough
hero.lead: Mission 25, The Battle of Rocky Island, Day 2, combines ground support with a later Shadow engagement and a headquarters assault. Protect the advancing troops throughout Operation Paint It Blue; an impressive opening attack is only part of the clear.
quickRoute: Open by attacking threats to the allied advance, using the active objective and troop reports to choose your next pass.
Keep air-to-air capability available for the Shadow engagement after the opening battle.
Return attention to the ground columns and remove the defenses blocking the headquarters approach.
Follow the marked final assault targets and the cease-fire order instead of continuing an old cleanup route.

sections.heading: Quick Mission 25 Strategy
paragraphs: Plan the sortie around the survival and movement of the ground force. Before selecting a distant target, ask which allied route it threatens and whether dealing with it changes the advance. The nearest red contact may be convenient but irrelevant to the unit currently taking fire. A short diversion to stop an active attacker can be more useful than finishing a tidy sweep of an already quiet sector.

Leave room in your loadout for a change of role. This battle asks you to attack surface defenses and then handle capable aircraft before returning to the ground assault. Spending every useful resource on the opening can leave the later fight unnecessarily slow. Build a plan that still works after the initial objective changes, and check the tactical display again whenever a new warning interrupts your attack.

sections.heading: Mission Objectives and Phases
paragraphs: The main clear concerns the capture of Sotoa’s headquarters. Allied ground forces approach on separate routes, so support cannot be reduced to one uninterrupted line of targets. Follow the reports of the unit in danger, then use the next quiet interval to move toward the other approach. Avoid inventing a fixed friendly health allowance: the warning and current objective are the useful information for your run.

The opening battle is followed by a Shadow fighter engagement, then renewed ground support and the final headquarters assault. Treat each transition as a fresh targeting problem. Confirm the new markers before using a scarce weapon; an attack that was useful a moment earlier may now take you away from the required battle.

table.caption: Mission 25 objective flow
rows: Reduce threats to the approaching troops
Recheck the objective when the opening period ends
Keep an effective air-to-air attack available
Do not lose track of the ground situation
Move when a different group needs help
Observe the final orders rather than chasing stragglers

sections.heading: Best Loadout for This Mission
paragraphs: A balanced aircraft is the practical starting point. Choose an airframe with surface-attack options and enough air capability to handle the interruption. Compare the weapons you can equip now instead of planning around a late unlock. If two aircraft both cover the roles, favor the one whose turning and attack recovery you can manage consistently. Losing an aircraft during a rushed pass costs more progress than a modest difference in weapon convenience.

For ground attacks, look for a special weapon that helps against the formations you can line up safely. For aircraft, keep an option you can employ without spending a long time chasing one opponent. Read the actual weapon description and target compatibility before sortieing. Do not assume that a weapon recommended for one role will lock onto every kind of target in the mission.

Think in terms of ammunition available at the next transition. If you used most of your air weapons before the Shadows arrived, test an opening that relies more on ground equipment and deliberate standard-missile attacks. If surface attacks are the weak point, improve alignment so each pass covers a useful group. Change one part of the loadout at a time to see which resource actually limits your clear.

steps.heading: Support the exposed approach
steps.description: Start with enemies capable of harming the advancing troops. Establish a clean line through one useful group, complete the attack, and check the allied reports before turning back. Do not remain over a cleared group while another approach comes under pressure.

steps.heading: Reset for the air battle
steps.description: When the Shadows become the active problem, recover enough space to maneuver and select your air weapon. Make deliberate attacks rather than firing through poor angles. Keep the ground force in your route planning so the dogfight does not become an excursion far from the battle.

steps.heading: Open the headquarters approach
steps.description: After the air threat is handled, return to the defenders holding up the ground force. Select the marked targets requested for the final assault. Confirm each update before moving to another sector, and stop when the mission orders a cease-fire.

sections.heading: Protecting Objectives and Target Priorities
paragraphs: If the mission fails while you still have plenty of ammunition, inspect your target order. Resources remaining at the end do not help a ground unit you left unsupported. On the next attempt, identify the first troop warning and alter the route before that point. This is a more useful correction than simply buying a heavier weapon and repeating the same sequence.

If troops seem stuck, look for the defenders around their current route and read the latest requested target. A stationary allied group is a signal to examine its immediate problem. Avoid assuming that every visible hostile must be cleared before it can move. Attack the relevant defenses, then watch for confirmation before leaving.

If you run out of useful weapons during the fighter battle, count the misses and unproductive pursuits from the previous attempt. You may need a different air weapon, but you may also need a steadier firing angle. If the loadout works against the first few aircraft, preserve that attack method instead of rushing the later engagements. Keep enough room to evade and set up another pass.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting and Replay Planning
paragraphs: Separate three replay goals: a reliable clear, a better rank, and optional collection. Each asks a different question. For a clear, find the first unsupported allied route. For rank improvement, compare attack efficiency and the time spent traveling between useful targets. For collection, check the relevant in-game record and plan the extra action without assuming it is required to capture the headquarters.

Write down the point at which your plan stopped matching the current objective. If it was the fighter transition, reserve a better air option. If it was the final advance, reduce unnecessary travel and return sooner. Keep the same difficulty while comparing attempts. Once the mission is secure, continue to Mission 26 or prepare for the Fatsia strike in Mission 27.

faq.question: Is Paint It Blue the name of Mission 25?
faq.answer: Paint It Blue is the operation name associated with Mission 25, The Battle of Rocky Island, Day 2. Use the number and mission title to distinguish it from the first day of the battle.

faq.question: Why can the ground assault fail while I am fighting aircraft?
faq.answer: Your ground-support responsibility still matters. Review the troop warnings and how far your dogfight carried you from the advance; respond to threats rather than following an aircraft indefinitely.

faq.question: Should I use only ground-attack weapons?
faq.answer: Keep an air-to-air option ready as well. The sortie includes a Shadow engagement between the opening battle and later headquarters support.

faq.question: What should I attack when friendly troops stop?
faq.answer: Check the latest objective and the hostile defenses around the stalled route. Remove the relevant blocker and watch for movement or an updated order before changing sectors.

faq.question: Do optional aces have to be part of my clear route?
faq.answer: Treat collection as a separate replay goal. Build a dependable headquarters-assault route first, then check the in-game records before adding optional detours.

title: Ace Combat 8 Mission 27 Walkthrough & Tips
description: Ace Combat 8 Mission 27 walkthrough: understand the objective order, plan your aircraft loadout, solve tricky phases, and improve your replay.

hero.heading: Ace Combat 8 Mission 27 Walkthrough
hero.lead: Mission 27, Fatsia, The Ocean Fortress, moves from attacks on the megafloat’s exterior to a central reactor objective. Structural targets help the opening battle; the later objective demands that you leave exterior cleanup behind.
quickRoute: Attack useful structural targets and explosive facilities instead of treating every exterior icon as equally valuable.
When the surrender and hold-fire orders arrive, stop shooting and read the changed objective.
Line up the central entrance with room to adjust before committing to the interior approach.
Attack the reactor as instructed and confirm the follow-up damage; do not assume the first hit completes the objective.

sections.heading: Mission 27 Quick Route
paragraphs: Build your route around the objective transitions. In the opening, look for an attack that changes the structure you are fighting over. Later, stop thinking in terms of the targets you left behind and start thinking about the central approach. Continuing a successful opening pattern after the mission changes is a common way to waste a run that was otherwise going well.

The first practical decision is choosing a manageable exterior sector. Work through targets from a clear attack line and watch what collapses or disappears. That gives you feedback about which attacks are producing useful progress. Do not fly into the structure simply to inspect the result. Recover to open space, check the next marker, and establish the next line from there.

sections.heading: Objectives in Order
paragraphs: Fatsia is a megafloat installation with exterior defenses and structural targets. Support pillars and explosive facilities are useful to the opening destruction plan. The battle subsequently reaches surrender orders and a central reactor objective. Follow the current order rather than imposing a requirement to remove every remaining exterior target.

Use the following table as a transition checklist. It deliberately avoids a fixed score or time requirement: read the displayed objective for the difficulty you selected. The important distinction is whether you should still be attacking the exterior, holding fire, or lining up for the interior. Confirm that distinction whenever dialogue interrupts the action.

table.caption: Fatsia transition checklist
rows: Circling isolated targets with no useful angle
Returning to an unfinished exterior arm
Read the target and make the required follow-up attack
Assuming an initial impact is the final confirmation

sections.heading: Aircraft and Special Weapon Choice
paragraphs: Start with a loadout that can handle dense surface targets while retaining control during the final approach. A surface weapon that reduces the number of exposed exterior passes can be useful, but the aircraft must still be comfortable to fly when the available space narrows. If you repeatedly collide inside, a familiar airframe is a sensible alternative to choosing only for destructive power.

Use the hangar to check weapon compatibility and your available reserve. Keep an air-capable option for threats that interrupt the surface attack. Do not commit every special weapon to targets already covered by an easy standard-missile pass. A balanced reserve gives you another answer when the approach you planned is blocked or when you need to recover from a missed attack.

For the reactor, favor a firing method you can line up and confirm. The size of an exterior target group is no reason to assume the same release pattern will work inside. Before entering, know which weapon is selected and which control changes that selection. Searching through options during a constrained turn is a preventable source of missed shots and collisions.

steps.heading: Create structural progress
steps.description: Choose a sector with a clear exit. Attack the relevant supports or explosive facilities, confirm the resulting destruction, and move along a planned line. Remove a defensive weapon when it prevents that line from being safe; do not turn every isolated gun into a separate low-level chase.

steps.heading: Obey the change of orders
steps.description: When surrender or hold-fire instructions arrive, stop the attack immediately. Read the next objective and move into position for the central approach. An old target remaining on screen is not permission to ignore the new order. Allow enough distance to align before entering.

steps.heading: Complete the reactor attack
steps.description: Inside, keep your attention on the marked reactor and the available firing window. An initial strike is followed by another attack before the shutter blocks the shot. Check the target feedback and mission confirmation, while keeping enough control to make the required turn rather than exploring side passages.

sections.heading: Handling Key Threats
paragraphs: Exterior defense and collision risk require different corrections. If gunfire disrupts every approach, clear the defense covering your chosen line or move to an angle with less exposure. If you hit the structure after a successful release, your recovery began too late. Give the next pass a defined exit and abandon the shot early if that exit disappears.

For the entrance, a longer setup is often easier to repeat than a last-second correction. Line up in open space, reduce the amount of bank needed at the opening, and keep the aircraft’s attitude readable. If the entrance drifts out of a safe line, reset before committing. Trying to rescue a bad entry from very close range can cost the entire attempt.

During the reactor sequence, distinguish a missed shot from incomplete damage. Check the selected target and visible feedback. If the first impact registers but the objective remains, prepare the follow-up rather than leaving to search for more exterior targets. Watch the shutter and current instructions; do not replace that information with an assumed number of seconds.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting a Failed Run
paragraphs: If you fail before reaching the interior, compare which exterior attacks created useful progress. Remove one unproductive detour and try the same sector again. If you reach the reactor reliably but fail there, retain the exterior route and practice the entry, target selection, and follow-up as one connected sequence. Changing the entire sortie at once makes it harder to tell what improved.

For rank replays, compare productive attacks, unnecessary exposure, and time spent reacquiring a target after each turn. Keep a successful clear as your reference instead of demanding a speculative numerical threshold. Mission 28 uses a different air-defense plan; continue to its dedicated guide rather than carrying Fatsia’s surface-attack loadout forward without review.

faq.question: Do I have to destroy every exterior target on Fatsia?
faq.answer: Follow the active destruction objective and its progress display. When the mission changes to hold fire or the central objective, stop exterior cleanup and follow that instruction.

faq.question: Why should I target supports and explosive facilities?
faq.answer: They can produce structural destruction, making them useful choices during the exterior battle. Check the result of the pass rather than assuming every red icon contributes equally to your route.

faq.question: What should I do when surrender is announced?
faq.answer: Stop shooting when ordered and check the new objective. Releasing the trigger also prevents a planned cleanup volley from carrying through the change of orders.

faq.question: Why did the reactor objective remain after my first hit?
faq.answer: The reactor sequence includes a follow-up attack. Check the target feedback and make the next required strike before the shutter obstructs it, rather than immediately returning outside.

faq.question: How can I make the interior approach safer?
faq.answer: Align from open space, select the intended weapon beforehand, and reset a poor approach before entering. Use an aircraft you can control consistently through the entry and turn.

title: Ace Combat 8 Mission 8 Walkthrough & Tips
description: Ace Combat 8 Mission 8 walkthrough with objective order, mission-stage advice, aircraft choices, common mistakes, and clear answers to player questions.

hero.heading: Ace Combat 8 Mission 8 Walkthrough
hero.lead: Mission 8 is Retaking of Theve II, Operation Gut Shot. Support the landing force, clear the ground advance, and intercept bombers before returning to the headquarters defenses. Keep the protected force at the center of your target decisions.
quickRoute: Check that the briefing reads Retaking of Theve II / Gut Shot; this guide uses the numbered Mission 08 route.
At the landing approach, attack threats to the friendly craft rather than pursuing distant fighters.
After landing, remove the defenses blocking allied ground units and respond to bomber warnings promptly.
Finish the marked headquarters defenders while preserving enough ammunition for later aircraft.

sections.heading: Mission 8 Quick Strategy
paragraphs: Start by identifying which friendly group you are supporting. As the landing develops, your useful target changes: a hostile aircraft near the craft, a defense blocking movement ashore, or a bomber on its approach can each become the immediate priority. Choose based on the current threat, not on the order in which red contacts first appeared on your screen.

Use each completed attack as a chance to read the next warning. A long turning fight can carry you away from the force you need to protect. If a target pulls you away without giving you a clean shot, reconsider the chase. Returning to the landing force may accomplish more than spending another circuit trying to finish that fighter. Your route should keep bringing you back to the active allied advance.

sections.heading: Mission Objectives
paragraphs: Retaking of Theve II mixes naval, ground, and air targets. The useful progression is landing support, assistance to the ground force, and attacks on the marked defenders around the headquarters. Bomber threats can interrupt that work. Follow the radio and objective display when they do; a stage summary should help interpret the mission, not override a new order.

When a ground unit stops, inspect the defenses along its route. Remove the target that prevents movement and watch for confirmation before moving elsewhere. During a bomber warning, reassess the air picture promptly. An escort trying to draw you into a turn is a different problem from the bomber continuing toward friendly troops.

table.caption: Mission 8 priority guide
rows: Remove the attacker threatening the craft
A fighter retreating away from the landing
Clear the defenses on its route
An unrelated target in a quiet area
A prolonged fight with its escort
Optional map cleanup away from the advance

sections.heading: Recommended Plane and Weapon Setup
paragraphs: Choose a multirole aircraft with a surface-attack option and a useful answer to airborne targets. A narrow surface-only plan makes the bomber interruptions harder, while an air-only setup can leave the ground advance slow. Compare the weapons you can equip on your current aircraft before treating another purchase as necessary. Familiar handling is valuable in a long sortie with frequent changes of target type.

Manage ammunition by the attack opportunities ahead. If a ground formation is lined up cleanly, use an appropriate weapon to avoid several separate turns. If targets are scattered, avoid spending a valuable area attack on one isolated vehicle simply because the weapon is ready. Preserve an air option for the next bomber warning instead of using all of it in the opening dogfight.

Check each weapon’s target compatibility in the hangar. During the sortie, verify the selected target after switching from surface to air combat. A failed lock may mean you still have the wrong weapon selected, rather than a problem with range. Practice that selection sequence before relying on it during a warning; the faster you can make the switch deliberately, the less likely you are to waste the first interception chance.

steps.heading: Keep the landing approach open
steps.description: Stay near enough to answer an attack on the friendly craft. Work through the threats affecting their approach, then look for the next active attacker. After each pass, check the craft rather than automatically turning back toward the last red contact you saw.

steps.heading: Unblock the ground advance
steps.description: Once troops are ashore, use their reports to find the group that cannot move. Attack the defenses directly affecting that route. When movement resumes, reassess the next group; staying over a solved blockage leaves other troops without support.

steps.heading: Interrupt for bombers
steps.description: A bomber warning changes the priority. Set up an intercept against the aircraft carrying the threat, and avoid letting an escort extend the chase. After the immediate air danger is handled, return to the ground objective and finish the marked headquarters defenses.

sections.heading: Common Problems and Fixes
paragraphs: If friendly losses end the run, find the moment you left the active objective unsupported. Were you fighting far away, attacking a quiet sector, or turning repeatedly over a target that no longer mattered? Change the route before that moment. Merely flying faster through the same detour may still leave too much time for the threatening unit to attack.

If you are shot down over ground defenses, shorten the exposure of each pass. Approach with enough room to identify the target, release from a stable line, and leave before beginning another turn. A tight circle directly above hostile defenses can make both aiming and threat awareness worse. A fresh approach also helps you see whether a new warning has appeared.

If ammunition is the limiting factor, identify the weapon and the stage where the shortage begins. Missiles spent on poor fighter angles call for better air attacks; surface weapons spent on isolated vehicles call for better grouping. Do not solve both problems with the same change by default. Retain the attacks that worked and replace the least productive part of the route.

sections.heading: Replay Advice
paragraphs: Learn a dependable support route before adding optional targets. On a first clear, the useful questions are whether the landing force stays protected and whether you reach the final defenders with a workable reserve. On a rank replay, compare the delay between a warning and your response, the number of unnecessary turns, and the amount of travel between active objectives.

Keep your aircraft and difficulty consistent for an initial comparison. If the next result improves, you can relate that improvement to the route change you made. If it gets worse, check whether the new shortcut actually left an allied group unsupported. Use the general S Rank guide for this replay method, then return to the mission list when choosing the next sortie.

faq.question: Is Mission 08 the same as Mission 8?
faq.answer: Yes. The leading zero is part of this site’s route format. The mission is Retaking of Theve II, with the operation name Gut Shot.

faq.question: Should I fight bomber escorts first?
faq.answer: Prioritize the bomber threatening friendly forces. Fight an escort when it prevents a safe interception, but avoid a long chase that leaves the bomber free to continue its attack.

faq.question: Why are my ground units not advancing?
faq.answer: Check their current report and the defenses along their route. Remove the relevant blocker, then look for movement or an objective update before leaving the area.

faq.question: What loadout fits Operation Gut Shot?
faq.answer: Use a manageable multirole aircraft with both surface and air capability. Keep ammunition available for bomber interruptions instead of committing everything to the opening targets.

faq.question: What should I change after running out of missiles?
faq.answer: Identify where the shortage started. Improve missed air shots or inefficient surface passes first, then consider capacity or a different weapon if the same stage still leaves you short.

title: Ace Combat 8 Mission 17 Walkthrough & Tips
description: Ace Combat 8 Mission 17 guide with objectives, recommended loadouts, walkthrough steps, key threats, replay tips, and answers to common questions.

hero.heading: Ace Combat 8 Mission 17 Walkthrough
hero.lead: Mission 17, Land Battleship No. 3, asks you to clear radar and surface-to-air defenses for the bomber attack. Work through the required targets along a planned route; the battleship itself is not a reason to abandon the marked defenses.
quickRoute: Read the remaining target groups and plan a continuous sweep rather than crossing the area repeatedly.
Attack the radar and SAM defenses required to open the bomber approach.
Recheck the target list around the land battleship when the objective updates.
Keep optional ace hunting separate from your first dependable clear and follow the bomber-related orders to completion.

sections.heading: Mission 17 Quick Plan
paragraphs: Start with the target display and your aircraft’s surface-attack options. Build a route through the marked defenses that leaves you lined up for the next group after each pass. Crossing back and forth for individual targets can consume the sortie without adding useful attacks. If you miss one, remember its position in relation to the next group rather than immediately making a hard turn under fire.

Keep the bomber-support purpose in mind. The mission is asking you to remove obstacles to another force’s attack, so optional opponents should not determine your route. Before chasing an aircraft, decide whether it is stopping you from completing the marked work. If it is only drawing you away, recover your attack line and continue clearing the required defenses.

sections.heading: Mission Goals and Phases
paragraphs: Land Battleship No. 3 is Operation Broncobuster. The opening work concerns radars and SAM launchers, followed by required targets near the battleship and the bomber attack. Use the objective changes as the boundary between these tasks. Do not import the mechanics of another land-battleship mission just because the large target looks familiar.

The safest planning aid is a short remaining-target check. After each pass, identify the next required group, the direction of your exit, and the weapon you will use. If the display still shows a defense you thought was destroyed, verify the actual target before spending another shot. A nearby visual explosion is less useful than confirmation that the marked objective has been removed.
